nodes.name: User and product owner
nodes.summary: Starts with a business idea and owns the intended outcome.
nodes.details: The user supplies an idea, clarifies the workload and reviews what the design means. The product is intended to help a person move from an early concept to a traceable baseline that an AWS engineer can develop further. The person stays outside the AWS service boundary and retains the decision to proceed.

aws.why: A person defines the need. Their identity would be authenticated separately by Amazon Cognito.
aws.notes: The user is not an AWS service. A sign-in session must not be interpreted as permission to provision cloud resources.

nodes.name: Sign-in and session boundary
nodes.summary: Protects workspace routes and private page operations.
nodes.details: The current Worker verifies the configured email and password, limits failed attempts and issues an eight-hour signed HttpOnly session cookie. A matching server-side session record is required. Logout removes that record. This is the current owner workspace, not a complete multi-customer account system. A multi-tenant service would also require an authorisation model for organisations, memberships and page ownership; those capabilities are not implemented by the current owner sign-in.

aws.why: A user pool is a candidate for managed application sign-in as this product gains separate customer accounts.
aws.notes: Authorise every page request by owner or tenant. Authentication does not itself provide tenant isolation. Keep browser sessions protected and retain server-side access checks.

nodes.details: The workspace shell owns the active page, current architecture view and selection. It coordinates fullscreen, the left canvas controls and the right study controls while retaining the starfield. Opening a drawer changes the interface, not the saved architecture by itself.

aws.why: The interactive shell remains browser JavaScript. CloudFront could deliver the application assets from an origin.
aws.notes: Do not move camera interaction to a server. Private APIs still need authentication, and protected responses must not enter a public cache.

nodes.name: Design identity and revisions
nodes.summary: Keep each design identity and stored revision context together.
nodes.details: Each current page has a stable ID, name, description, architecture reference, selected view, optional layers and update time. The product direction extends this into immutable accepted revisions with a draft pointer, author and source lineage. Agentic Core models remain separate from the System Architecture Workspace product model. A saved page is structured design data, not deployed infrastructure.

aws.why: DynamoDB is a possible future application store for per-owner page records and their revision metadata.
aws.notes: Use an explicit tenant or owner key and a revision condition for writes. Keep GitHub as the current private version history until a deliberate data migration is approved.

nodes.name: Public entry and portfolio
nodes.summary: Introduces the product and provides sign-in and portfolio navigation.
nodes.details: The public entry presents the workspace idea, a teal galaxy and the portfolio. Its navigation changes the entry view without loading a second animated galaxy. Access to the introduction is public, while the workspace and its private data still require sign-in.

aws.why: S3 can hold static entry assets, with CloudFront delivering them to visitors.
aws.notes: Separate public assets from protected design data. The application must not bundle private repository content or credentials into public JavaScript.

nodes.name: Loading and fullscreen transition
nodes.summary: Moves successful sign-in into the workspace with the existing five-second experience.
nodes.details: Sign-in requests fullscreen during the user gesture. After authentication succeeds, the existing galaxy moves into the loading presentation for five seconds. The workspace then loads. If fullscreen is accepted, a same-origin frame preserves it; otherwise the site navigates normally. Hidden entry animations stop when the workspace takes over.
outputs: Workspace entry after the loading presentation

aws.why: This is a browser experience, not a separate AWS service. The hosting layer only supplies its files.
aws.notes: Fullscreen remains subject to the browser. The transition must never bypass sign-in or hide an authentication error.

nodes.name: Editable 3D system model
nodes.summary: Make components, interfaces and dependencies inspectable.
nodes.details: Today the browser renders manually authored architecture datasets with orbit, selection and contextual explanations. The product direction is to turn a confirmed brief into an editable graph whose nodes represent responsibilities and whose directed edges represent interfaces or data flows. The 3D brain is a way to inspect this structured model; spatial proximity is not proof of a dependency. Generated editing and prompt-to-model creation remain proposed.

aws.why: Rendering remains on the user device. CloudFront could deliver application and model assets while protected APIs serve private records.
aws.notes: Browser graphics are not an AWS service. Use bounded scene work, pause hidden rendering and preserve a keyboard-accessible way to inspect every component.

nodes.name: Browser draft retention
nodes.summary: Keep local page state available between visits.
nodes.details: The browser retains current page records and view choices locally. The stored format is portable JSON, and the retained data adapter validates supported records. Page settings and its file controls are removed from this presentation. Browser data remains local to this device and can be cleared by the user or browser; it is not a confirmed GitHub save or a multi-device backup.

aws.why: Local drafts should still work in the browser. S3 could store optional durable exports in a future cloud account.
aws.notes: A local write is not a server receipt. Show unsynced changes clearly and avoid uploading a draft until the user requests a save.

nodes.name: Private page storage API
nodes.summary: Validates and mediates explicit reads and saves to the private repository.
nodes.details: The current Worker exposes status, connect, list, read and save routes under /api/workspace-store. It requires a valid session, rejects cross-origin writes, validates page fields and sizes, and checks repository privacy. GitHub updates use the last-read file SHA so a conflicting revision requires review rather than silent replacement.

aws.why: API Gateway could expose the authenticated endpoints and Lambda could perform the validation and GitHub calls.
aws.notes: Retain same-origin browser controls, request limits, ownership checks and revision conditions. A successful API request must still include a trustworthy save receipt.

nodes.details: The existing server adapter encrypts a repository-scoped GitHub token with AES-GCM before storing it in the archive binding and decrypts it only for server-side calls. Secrets must stay outside public assets, browser storage and diagnostic logs.

nodes.name: Worker routing and request handling
nodes.summary: Serves the public entry, protects workspace routes and dispatches APIs.
nodes.details: The current website uses an edge Worker. Non-public content is served only after session validation. Errors return bounded responses rather than exposing internals.

aws.why: An AWS migration could divide static delivery, API routing and request logic between these services.
aws.notes: This is a proposed migration from the current Worker. Preserve route semantics, private cache policy and authentication checks rather than assuming hosting changes are equivalent.

nodes.name: Archive and session storage
nodes.summary: Provides server-side storage used by the current Worker.
nodes.details: The ARCHIVE binding stores private large files, session records, failed-attempt state and the encrypted repository connection. Small static files are embedded by the build. Each purpose has different retention and access needs, so an AWS migration should separate object storage, session state and secrets rather than copying them into one undifferentiated bucket.

aws.why: S3 suits private object files; DynamoDB is a candidate for session and application state. Credentials belong in Secrets Manager.
aws.notes: Session validity must be checked on every protected request. Object retention and session expiry are different requirements, even if the current binding stores both.

nodes.name: AWS engineer review
nodes.summary: Bring human engineering judgement into the handoff.
nodes.details: An AWS engineer reviews the candidate against actual security, networking, tenancy, availability, data retention, recovery and cost requirements. Infrastructure as code needs linting, policy checks, account-specific planning and isolated testing before a separate deployment decision. Approval records must identify the exact brief and model revision; a changed model needs a new review.

overview.title: From an idea to an engineer-reviewed AWS baseline
overview.summary: Shape a requirement, explore its 3D system model and turn a reviewed design into a baseline AWS engineers can build on.
overview.current: The working prototype provides sign-in, selectable pages, interactive 3D reference models, contextual explanations, proposed AWS mappings and browser-retained design records. Its current free guide retrieves recorded information. The website runs on a Worker, not on the proposed AWS stack.
overview.approach: The core view explains the intended product journey. The supporting groups expose the current website and the proposed platform services. This manually authored system design is assessed through requirements, interfaces, implementation checks and review, without a mathematical-proof claim.

workflow.title: 1. User and product owner
workflow.detail: Starts with a business idea and owns the intended outcome.

workflow.title: 2. Idea and requirements brief
workflow.detail: Make the idea specific enough to design and review.

workflow.title: 3. Editable 3D system model
workflow.detail: Make components, interfaces and dependencies inspectable.

workflow.title: 4. Schema checks and design findings
workflow.detail: Expose missing, inconsistent or unsafe assumptions before AWS mapping.

workflow.title: 5. AWS architecture synthesis
workflow.detail: Translate the reviewed model into justified AWS responsibilities.

workflow.title: 6. AWS engineer review
workflow.detail: Bring human engineering judgement into the handoff.

workflow.title: 7. Reviewed AWS baseline package
workflow.detail: Deliver a traceable starting architecture for AWS engineers.

overview.aws: This is a proposed AWS target for the product, not a deployed environment. CloudFront and S3 deliver assets, Cognito provides application identity, API Gateway and Lambda serve authenticated APIs, DynamoDB stores tenant-scoped design metadata, Bedrock drafts candidate models, Step Functions coordinates jobs and human review, and S3 retains baseline bundles. Private GitHub remains the current revision store. Service choices require workload and regional validation before implementation.
failures: Incomplete brief: ask the user to resolve missing requirements before starting generation.
Invalid generated model: retain the candidate and return explicit schema or design findings.
Job timeout or model error: record a resumable failure, use bounded retries and preserve the input revision.
Concurrent edit: reject a stale write and preserve both revisions for review.
Engineer rejects the AWS candidate: return findings to a new revision without releasing the baseline.
Private storage unavailable: show unsaved status and preserve the local draft; do not claim a successful save.
boundaries: Implemented prototype: manually authored 3D models, sign-in, page selection, study panels and local page retention.
Private GitHub: repository created; runtime operations require a server connection.
Proposed product pipeline: prompt-to-model, automated checks, AWS synthesis and formal engineer review.
Proposed AWS infrastructure: architecture options, not deployed services.
Final output: a reviewed starting baseline, not production certification or automatic deployment.

operational.title: Identity and tenant isolation
operational.detail: Authenticate the user, derive tenant identity from trusted claims and authorise every record, job and download. Isolation needs independent tests; a Cognito login is only one part of the boundary.

operational.title: Schema and versioning
operational.detail: Store stable design IDs, schema versions, immutable accepted revisions and source lineage. Use conditional writes, recoverable migrations and review decisions tied to exact revisions.

operational.title: Asynchronous jobs
operational.detail: Use durable job IDs, idempotency keys, bounded retries, timeouts, cancellation handling and visible failure states. Keep the interface responsive while work runs.

operational.title: Validation and handoff
operational.detail: Separate model suggestions, deterministic findings, human review and deployment authority. Candidate infrastructure as code needs linting, policy checks and testing in an isolated account before use.

operational.title: Cost and operations
operational.detail: Set tenant usage quotas and model budgets, measure latency and failures, protect prompt content in logs, define retention and test backup and restore. Validate cost assumptions using the actual workload.

overview.vision: Help people explain an idea, inspect a structured 3D brain and create a traceable AWS baseline that shortens the engineer’s discovery work. Validate that benefit with pilots, measured review time, design quality and engineer feedback.

evidence.scope: Historical design/source-review statements from the pinned design-data snapshot. This public data export is not application source, a new runtime verification or an AWS deployment receipt. See docs/PROVENANCE.md for the separate Site v81 source identity.
